penguins |>
  filter(is.na(body_mass_g) | is.na(flipper_length_mm)) |>

  species body_mass_g flipper_length_mm

The table has 344 penguins. There are 2 missing values in body_mass_g and 2 in flipper_length_mm.

penguin_sizes <- penguins |>
  select(species, body_mass_g, flipper_length_mm) |>
  drop_na()
nrow(penguin_sizes)

[1] 342


Dropping rows with missing values leaves 342 penguins, so the missing values must belong to the same two penguins.

title: Using R with Quarto to analyse penguin size and flipper length
text:
Summarise size by species

summary_by_species <- penguin_sizes |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(
    number_of_penguins = n(),
    mean_mass_g = round(mean(body_mass_g), 1),
    mean_flipper_mm = round(mean(flipper_length_mm), 1)
  )
summary_by_species

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  species   number_of_penguins mean_mass_g mean_flipper_mm
  <fct>                  <int>       <dbl>           <dbl>
1 Adelie                   151       3701.            190 
2 Chinstrap                 68       3733.            196.
3 Gentoo                   123       5076             217.


Adelie and Chinstrap penguins are almost the same mass, about 3700 g on average. Gentoo penguins are much heavier at about 5076 g, and they also have the longest flippers, about 217 mm.

title: Using R with Quarto to analyse penguin size and flipper length
section: Plot flipper length against body mass
text:
Plot flipper length against body mass

ggplot(penguin_sizes, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Body mass (g)", colour = "Species")







Figure 1: Body mass against flipper length, coloured by species.

title: Using R with Quarto to analyse penguin size and flipper length
text:
Conclusion
Figure 1 shows that penguins with longer flippers tend to be heavier. Gentoo penguins form their own cluster at the top right because they are the largest on both measures. Adelie and Chinstrap overlap heavily.
This shows an association between the two measurements only. It does not show that one causes the other, and I did not test the relationship formally.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
Three weeks ago I moved from the UK to Vancouver to start the Master of Data Science at UBC. Coming back to full-time study after several years of working was a strange adjustment. I’d forgotten the rhythm of lectures, labs and deadlines stacked on top of each other. Orientation and the first week of classes went by faster than I expected, and it took a while to stop thinking in terms of project timelines and start thinking in terms of weekly labs.
The pace has been the biggest surprise. I came in expecting the statistics to be the hard part and the tooling to be familiar, and it’s been closer to the opposite: the volume of new programming tools, languages and tech stacks in the first few weeks has been relentless. My cohort has made that much easier, and some of the most useful things I’ve picked up have come out of working through problems with the people around me rather than from the lectures themselves.
Three weeks in, I’m tired but genuinely enjoying it. The parts I’m most looking forward to are still ahead, I want to get into the modelling courses and start applying this to real problems rather than exercises. So far my free time has been limited, but I’m hoping to settle in soon and see more of Vancouver and BC.

title: About

Why data science
Architecting decisioning systems meant I spent years close to the models that drove them without ever owning the modelling itself, and moving into a management role only sharpened that. As the field has evolved those models have become steadily more central to how decisioning works, and analysing them was consistently the part of the job I enjoyed most. I came to UBC’s Master of Data Science to build a broader and deeper foundation than I could pick up on the job, and to work with methods I was unlikely to meet in the marketing projects I was on.

title: Using Python with Quarto to analyse penguin size and flipper length
section: Plot flipper length against body mass
text:
Plot flipper length against body mass

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))

for species, group in penguin_sizes.groupby("species"):
    ax.scatter(group["flipper_length_mm"], group["body_mass_g"],
               label=species)

ax.set_xlabel("Flipper length (mm)")
ax.set_ylabel("Body mass (g)")
ax.legend(title="Species")
plt.show()







Figure 1: Body mass against flipper length with penguins by species.

title: Using Python with Quarto to analyse penguin size and flipper length
text:
Conclusion
Figure 1 shows a clear upward trend between body mass and flipper, as body masse increases so does flipper length. Gentoo penguins form their own cluster at the top right as the are the biggest for both metrics. Adelie and Chinstrap on ther other hand overlap heavily.
This analysis shows that there is some association between the two but further work needs to establish the relationship more rigorously.
